catalog_quote: [p.19, sec. 4.2.3 Words with minor syllables] The term sesquisyllable, which is derived from the Latin sesqui- meaning “one and a half,” was coined by Matisoff (1973) to describe a phonological unit characteristic of many Southeast Asian languages. It consists of a major syllable which is fully stressed, vowel rich, and tone bearing, preceded by an unstressed minor syllable or presyllable ((Matisoff, 1973, p. 86). When two minor syllables occur in a word, the first minor syllable always functions as the negative marker, while the second is an inherent part of the lexical base. This creates a fixed Minor–Minor–Major template. The negative prefix a- or d- occupies the initial slot, preceding the transitional sound such as l- of the root, as you can see in examples (4) and (5). ... In these cases, both syllables remain unstressed and phonologically reduced. The language also allows minor syllables to appear between major syllables. [p.14, sec. 4.1.1] Since Gongvangpounyiu is a tonal language, T represents tone. ... In this language, all major syllables carry tone. [p.16, sec. 4.1.2] The study observed that the minor syllables do not carry contrastive tones, but they exhibit variations in pitch. However, more investigation for the study is required. [p.29, sec. 5.3] There are six contrastive lexical tones. It is observed that there are three level tones: high, mid, and low. The contour tones are high to low falling, mid to low falling, and rising.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gongvangpounyiu is a tone language (six contrastive tones, borne by every major syllable). Words are monosyllabic, compounds of major syllables, or sesquisyllabic: minor syllables (V or C+schwa, always open, toneless) are unstressed and reduced, and the following major (full, tone-bearing) syllable carries the stress, i.e. word-final prominence in minor+major and minor+minor+major words. The thesis makes no claim about relative stress among the major syllables of compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: Minor syllables may also occur between major syllables inside compounds (Table 7); minor syllables show non-contrastive pitch variation possibly conditioned by the following major syllable's tone (flagged for future research); one speaker realised tone 31 as 11 in isolation vs 31 in a carrier phrase.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms from a 2,524-item wordlist recorded in isolation, three repetitions, plus minimal pairs in a carrier frame; two speakers of the Pounyiu variety). Stress characterisation is structural (major vs minor syllable), not instrumental.
new_statements.identity_note: Methiam 2026 describes the Pounyiu variety (community standard for the orthography; author from Pounyiu Nuakgong, Lahe Township, Naga Self-Administered Zone, Sagaing) of what the community calls Gongvangpounyiu = Glottolog pony1234 'Pounyiu-Gongvan Naga' = ISO npg 'Ponyo-Gongwang Naga'. Speakers recognise two dialect groups, Pounyiu and Gongvang (88-89% lexical similarity), each with three sub-varieties; Gongvang itself is not separately described. Glottolog lists no dialect-level codes.

sources.note: Tonal (6 contrastive tones on major syllables). Words are sesquisyllabic: minor syllables (V or C+schwa) are unstressed, open, phonologically reduced and carry no contrastive tone; the major syllable is 'fully stressed, vowel rich, and tone bearing' (p.19, citing Matisoff's definition and applying it; NEG-prefix + minor + major words: 'both [minor] syllables remain unstressed'). No statement on relative prominence among major syllables of compounds. Body pages 8-40 have no usable text layer; read via 300-dpi tesseract scanned and page images (quote verified against image).
